claim: During herpesvirus infection, egress of nascent viral capsids from the nucleus is mediated by the viral nuclear egress complex (NEC).
source: During herpesvirus infection, egress of nascent viral capsids from the nucleus is mediated by the viral nuclear egress complex (NEC).
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the field, supported by citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: NEC deforms the inner nuclear membrane (INM) around the capsid by forming a hexagonal array.
source: NEC deforms the inner nuclear membrane (INM) around the capsid by forming a hexagonal array.
evidence: This is supported by previous structural studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: Binding of the capsid protein UL25 promotes the formation of NEC pentagons rather than hexagons.
source: Here, by structure-guided truncations, confocal microscopy, and cryoelectron tomography, we show that binding of the capsid protein UL25 promotes the formation of NEC pentagons rather than hexagons.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data from confocal microscopy and cryoelectron tomography presented in the manuscript.

claim: UL25 is situated at the pentagonal capsid vertices.
source: binding of UL25 situated at the pentagonal capsid vertices to the NEC at the INM promotes formation of NEC pentagons
evidence: This is supported by previous structural studies of herpesvirus capsids.

claim: Incorporation of NEC pentagons at the points of contact with the vertices would promote assembly of the curved hexagonal NEC coat around the capsid.
source: Incorporation of NEC pentagons at the points of contact with the vertices would also promote assembly of the curved hexagonal NEC coat around the capsid, leading to productive egress of UL25-decorated capsids.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the experimental observations and structural modeling presented in the manuscript.

claim: All herpesviruses can establish lifelong, latent infections within the host.
source: All herpesviruses can establish lifelong, latent infections within the host, from which they can periodically reactivate, spreading to uninfected tissues and hosts and causing a number of ailments.
evidence: This is established knowledge about herpesvirus biology.

claim: Nuclear capsids bud at the inner nuclear membrane (INM) forming enveloped vesicles that pinch off into the perinuclear space.
source: First, nuclear capsids bud at the inner nuclear membrane (INM) forming enveloped vesicles that pinch off into the perinuclear space.
evidence: This is a well-established step in herpesvirus egress, supported by citations.

claim: Perinuclear enveloped virions fuse with the outer nuclear membrane, which releases the capsids into the cytosol.
source: These perinuclear enveloped virions fuse with the outer nuclear membrane, which releases the capsids into the cytosol.
evidence: This is a well-established step in herpesvirus egress.

claim: Herpesviruses are unusual among vertebrate viruses in their ability to bud at the nuclear envelope.
source: herpesviruses are unusual among vertebrate viruses in their ability to bud at the nuclear envelope (Bigalke and Heldwein, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: Capsid budding at the nuclear envelope requires two conserved herpesviral proteins, UL31 and UL34 in HSV-1.
source: Capsid budding at the nuclear envelope requires two conserved herpesviral proteins, which are named UL31 and UL34 in herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1), that form the nuclear egress complex (NEC) (reviewed in Bigalke and Heldwein, 2016; Bigalke and Heldwein, 2017; Mettenleiter et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to review articles.

claim: The NEC heterodimer is anchored at the INM through the single C-terminal transmembrane helix of UL34.
source: The NEC heterodimer is anchored at the INM through the single C-terminal transmembrane helix of UL34 and faces the nucleoplasm (Shiba et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: UL31 is a nuclear phosphoprotein that colocalizes with UL34.
source: UL31 is a nuclear phosphoprotein that colocalizes with UL34 (Chang and Roizman, 1993; Reynolds et al., 2001)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: UL31 interacts with the capsid during nuclear egress.
source: UL31 is a nuclear phosphoprotein that colocalizes with UL34 (Chang and Roizman, 1993; Reynolds et al., 2001) and interacts with the capsid during nuclear egress (Trus et al., 2007; Yang and Baines, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Both UL31 and UL34 are necessary for efficient nuclear egress.
source: Both UL31 and UL34 are necessary for efficient nuclear egress, and in the absence of either protein, capsids accumulate in the nucleus and viral replication is reduced by several orders of magnitude (Fuchs et al., 2002; Roller et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: HSV-1 NEC has an intrinsic ability to deform and bud membranes.
source: Previously, we discovered that HSV-1 NEC has an intrinsic ability to deform and bud membranes by demonstrating that purified recombinant NEC vesiculates synthetic lipid bilayers in vitro without any additional factors or chemical energy (Bigalke et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: Purified recombinant NEC vesiculates synthetic lipid bilayers in vitro without any additional factors or chemical energy.
source: purified recombinant NEC vesiculates synthetic lipid bilayers in vitro without any additional factors or chemical energy (Bigalke et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The NEC forms hexagonal 'honeycomb' coats on the inner surface of budded vesicles formed in vitro.
source: Using cryogenic electron microscopy and tomography (cryoEM/ET), we showed that the NEC forms hexagonal 'honeycomb' coats on the inner surface of budded vesicles formed in vitro (Bigalke et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: Very similar hexagonal coats were observed in capsidless perinuclear vesicles formed in vivo, in uninfected cells expressing PRV NEC.
source: Very similar hexagonal coats were observed in capsidless perinuclear vesicles formed in vivo, in uninfected cells expressing PRV NEC (Hagen et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: HSV-1 NEC formed a hexagonal lattice of the same dimensions in crystals.
source: Additionally, HSV-1 NEC formed a hexagonal lattice of the same dimensions in crystals (Bigalke and Heldwein, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: Mutations that disrupt oligomeric interfaces reduce budding in vitro and in vivo.
source: subsequent work confirmed that mutations that disrupt oligomeric interfaces reduce budding in vitro (Bigalke and Heldwein, 2015; Bigalke et al., 2014) and in vivo (Arii et al., 2019; Roller et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: A purely hexagonal arrangement is flat.
source: A purely hexagonal arrangement is flat, so curvature is typically achieved either by insertions of pentagons as found at 12 vertices of an icosahedron (Zandi et al., 2004), or by inclusion of irregular defects as observed in several viral coats (Briggs et al., 2009; Heuser, 2005; Hyun et al., 2011; Schur et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge in structural biology, supported by citations.

claim: Curvature in hexagonal arrangements is typically achieved either by insertions of pentagons or by inclusion of irregular defects.
source: A purely hexagonal arrangement is flat, so curvature is typically achieved either by insertions of pentagons as found at 12 vertices of an icosahedron (Zandi et al., 2004), or by inclusion of irregular defects as observed in several viral coats (Briggs et al., 2009; Heuser, 2005; Hyun et al., 2011; Schur et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge in structural biology, supported by citations.

claim: In perinuclear vesicles visualized in infected cells, the NEC coats appear to be tightly associated with the capsid.
source: In perinuclear visualized in infected cells, the NEC coats appear to be tightly associated with the capsid (Hagen et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Capsid interactions with the NEC during nuclear budding may be mediated by binding of the capsid protein UL25 to UL31.
source: Capsid interactions with the NEC during nuclear budding may be mediated by binding of the capsid protein UL25 to UL31 (Yang and Baines, 2011; Yang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: UL25 forms pentagonal complexes at the vertices of the icosahedral herpesvirus capsids.
source: Moreover, UL25 forms pentagonal complexes at the vertices of the icosahedral herpesvirus capsids (Dai and Zhou, 2018; Furlong, 1978).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: HSV-1 UL25 can be expressed in soluble form in E. coli only when residues 1–44 are deleted.
source: HSV-1 UL25 can be expressed in soluble form in E. coli only when residues 1–44 are deleted (Bowman et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Residues 1–50 of UL25 are necessary and sufficient for capsid binding.
source: Residues 1–50 are necessary and sufficient for capsid binding (Cockrell et al., 2009)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: In the cryoEM structure of the HSV-1 capsid, UL25 residues 1-50 mediate extensive interactions with another capsid protein, UL17.
source: in the cryoEM structure of the HSV-1 capsid, these residues mediate extensive interactions with another capsid protein, UL17 (Dai and Zhou, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: UL25∆44 was proteolytically cleaved during purification despite the presence of protease inhibitors.
source: UL25∆44 was soluble and could be purified, in agreement with the previous report (Bowman et al., 2006), but was proteolytically cleaved during purification despite the presence of protease inhibitors (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: N-terminal sequencing of the UL25∆44 proteolytic product by Edman degradation yielded the amino acid sequence AAELPV, corresponding to residues 73–78.
source: N-terminal sequencing of the single proteolytic product by Edman degradation yielded the amino acid sequence AAELPV, corresponding to residues 73–78.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Edman degradation sequencing.

claim: UL25∆44 was cleaved between residues Q72 and A73.
source: This suggested that UL25∆44 was cleaved between residues Q72 and A73.
evidence: This is inferred from the N-terminal sequencing data.

claim: UL25∆44 Q72A and UL25∆73 constructs yielded a single UL25 species after purification.
source: Both constructs yielded a single UL25 species after purification (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: UL25∆44 Q72A inhibited NEC-mediated budding in a dose-dependent manner.
source: UL25∆44 Q72A inhibited NEC-mediated budding in a dose-dependent manner, and at 1:10 or 1:20 NEC:UL25 molar ratios, few budding events were observed (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: UL25∆73 did not inhibit budding even at a 1:20 ratio of NEC:UL25.
source: By contrast, UL25∆73 did not inhibit budding even at a 1:20 ratio of NEC:UL25 (Figure 1c)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: Residues 45–73 of UL25 are necessary for inhibition of NEC-mediated budding.
source: which suggested that residues 45–73 were necessary for inhibition.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of UL25∆44 Q72A and UL25∆73 budding inhibition data.

claim: UL25∆44 consists of a long N-terminal α-helix (residues 48–94), followed by a flexible linker unresolved in the cryoEM structure, and a C-terminal globular core (residues 134–580).
source: UL25∆44 consists of a long N-terminal α-helix (residues 48–94), followed by a flexible linker unresolved in the cryoEM structure, and a C-terminal globular core (residues 134–580) (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is based on the cryoEM structure of capsid-bound UL25, shown in Figure 1a.

claim: Residues 45–73 of UL25 encompass the N-terminal half of the long α-helix.
source: Residues 45–73 encompass the N-terminal half of the long α-helix.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural information about UL25.

claim: Residues 61–69 of UL25 form a highly conserved alanine-rich region.
source: Sequence alignment of UL25 homologs from five alphaherpesviruses revealed a divergent N terminus followed by a highly conserved alanine-rich region, residues 61–69 (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 1a.

claim: UL25∆58 Q72A did not inhibit NEC220 budding.
source: UL25∆58 Q72A did not inhibit NEC220 budding (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: UL25∆50 Q72A inhibited budding at a 1:10 NEC:UL25 ratio.
source: We also generated a UL25∆50 Q72A construct (as a control for studies using eGFP-UL25 chimera described below), which inhibited budding at a 1:10 NEC:UL25 ratio, the minimal UL25 concentration for budding inhibition (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Residues 51–73 of UL25 are essential for inhibition of NEC-mediated budding.
source: Thus, residues 51–73 appear essential for inhibition, whereas residues 45–50 are dispensable.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of different UL25 truncation constructs and their effects on budding.

claim: UL25∆44 Q72A did not bind synthetic lipid vesicles.
source: Unlike NEC220, UL25∆44 Q72A did not bind synthetic lipid vesicles (Figure 1d)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from co-sedimentation assays shown in Figure 1d.

claim: UL25 does not compete with the NEC220 for binding to membranes.
source: and, therefore, could not compete with the NEC220 for binding to membranes.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that UL25 does not bind membranes.

claim: No binding was detected between UL25∆44 and NEC220 by isothermal titration calorimetry.
source: However, no binding was detected in solution, either between UL25∆44 and NEC220 by isothermal titration calorimetry (Figure 1—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from ITC shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: No binding was detected between UL25∆44 and NEC185∆50 by size-exclusion chromatography.
source: or between UL25∆44 and NEC185∆50 [a truncated construct that was crystallized previously (Bigalke and Heldwein, 2015)] by size-exclusion chromatography (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from size-exclusion chromatography shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: To bind UL25, NEC may need to be bound to the membrane.
source: Therefore, to bind UL25, NEC may need to be bound to the membrane.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that UL25 and NEC do not interact in solution but do interact when NEC is membrane-bound.

claim: eGFP-UL25∆50 Q72A efficiently inhibited NEC-mediated budding.
source: eGFP-UL25∆50 Q72A (as well as its untagged version UL25∆50 Q72A) efficiently inhibited NEC-mediated budding, whereas eGFP-UL25∆73 did not (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: eGFP-UL25∆73 did not inhibit NEC-mediated budding.
source: eGFP-UL25∆50 Q72A (as well as its untagged version UL25∆50 Q72A) efficiently inhibited NEC-mediated budding, whereas eGFP-UL25∆73 did not (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: When eGFP-tagged UL25 constructs were incubated with fluorescently labelled GUVs, no eGFP signal was detected on the GUV membranes.
source: When eGFP-tagged UL25 constructs were incubated with the fluorescently labelled GUVs, no eGFP signal was detected on the GUV membranes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), confirming that UL25 did not bind membranes directly.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: In the presence of NEC220, eGFP-UL25∆50 colocalized with the GUV membranes.
source: In the presence of the NEC220, the eGFP-UL25∆50 colocalized with the GUV membranes, and very little budding was detected (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: Very little budding was detected when eGFP-UL25∆50 was incubated with GUVs in the presence of NEC220.
source: In the presence of the NEC220, the eGFP-UL25∆50 colocalized with the GUV membranes, and very little budding was detected (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: eGFP-UL25∆50 binds NEC that is bound to the surface of the GUVs.
source: UL25 itself does not bind membranes, so, instead, it must be binding NEC that is bound to the surface of the GUVs.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that eGFP-UL25∆50 colocalizes with GUV membranes only in the presence of NEC.

claim: In the presence of NEC220, eGFP-UL25∆73 colocalized with the GUV membranes.
source: In the presence of the NEC220, eGFP-UL25∆73 also colocalized with the GUV membranes.
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations described in the text.

claim: The eGFP signal from eGFP-UL25∆73 was sometimes detected on the membranes of intraluminal vesicles (ILVs) inside the GUVs.
source: In this case, the eGFP signal was sometimes detected on the membranes of intraluminal vesicles (ILVs) inside the GUVs (Figure 2c)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: Binding of eGFP-UL25∆73 to the NEC220 did not interfere with budding.
source: which confirmed that binding of eGFP-UL25∆73 to the NEC220 did not interfere with budding (Figure 2a)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: eGFP-UL25∆73 could remain bound to the NEC-coated membranes throughout budding.
source: and that eGFP-UL25∆73 could even remain bound to the NEC-coated membranes throughout budding.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that eGFP-UL25∆73 is detected on ILVs, which are products of budding.

claim: eGFP-UL25∆73 was clustered around the unbudded GUVs, probably due to its aggregation.
source: In many cases, however, the eGFP-UL25∆73 was clustered around the unbudded GUVs, probably due to its aggregation (Figure 2d).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2d.

claim: Aggregation of eGFP-UL25∆73 was not observed for eGFP-UL25∆50 Q72A.
source: Such aggregation was not observed for eGFP-UL25∆50 Q72A (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: Residues D275, K279, and D282 at the membrane-distal tip of UL31 have been implicated in capsid binding in PRV.
source: Residues D275, K279, and D282 at the membrane-distal tip of UL31 have been implicated in capsid binding in PRV (Rönfeldt et al., 2017) and in HSV-1 (Takeshima et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Residues D275, K279, and D282 at the membrane-distal tip of UL31 have been implicated in capsid binding in HSV-1.
source: Residues D275, K279, and D282 at the membrane-distal tip of UL31 have been implicated in capsid binding in PRV (Rönfeldt et al., 2017) and in HSV-1 (Takeshima et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: NEC220-CBM mediated budding at levels similar to the WT NEC220.
source: The corresponding mutant NEC220, termed capsid-binding mutant (NEC220-CBM), mediated budding at levels similar to the WT NEC220 (Figure 3a)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: NEC220-CBM was much less sensitive to inhibition by UL25∆44 Q72A than WT NEC220.
source: but was much less sensitive to inhibition by UL25∆44 Q72A (Figure 3a) as demonstrated by the 25% reduction in budding of NEC220-CBM compared to 75% for NEC220 (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3a and Figure 1c.

claim: eGFP-UL25∆50 Q72A did not co-localize with the GUV membranes in the presence of the NEC220-CBM.
source: Moreover, eGFP-UL25∆50 Q72A did not co-localize with the GUV membranes in the presence of the NEC220-CBM (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: UL25∆44 Q72A binds to the membrane-distal tip of UL31.
source: These results suggested that UL25∆44 Q72A bound to the membrane-distal tip of UL31 and that this interaction was essential for its inhibitory activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that mutations at the membrane-distal tip of UL31 reduce UL25 binding and inhibition.

claim: The interaction between UL25∆44 Q72A and the membrane-distal tip of UL31 is essential for UL25's inhibitory activity.
source: These results suggested that UL25∆44 Q72A bound to the membrane-distal tip of UL31 and that this interaction was essential for its inhibitory activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that mutations at the membrane-distal tip of UL31 reduce UL25 binding and inhibition.

claim: NEC-mediated budding of synthetic large unilamellar vesicles (LUVs) resulted in the formation of smaller vesicles containing ~11 nm thick internal NEC coats.
source: Previously, we showed that NEC-mediated budding of synthetic large unilamellar vesicles (LUVs) resulted in the formation of smaller vesicles containing ~11 nm thick internal NEC coats (Bigalke et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: In the presence of UL25∆44 Q72A and NEC220, the LUVs were mostly spherical, and their external surface was coated with ~17 nm thick coats.
source: In the presence of UL25∆44 Q72A and NEC220, the LUVs were mostly spherical, and their external surface was coated with ~17 nm thick coats (Figure 4a)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: The external coats formed in the presence of UL25∆44 Q72A were ~6 nm thicker than the internal NEC coats.
source: The external coats formed in the presence of UL25∆44 Q72A were ~6 nm thicker than the internal NEC coats, and the diameter of the globular portion of UL25 is also ~6 nm.
evidence: This is based on measurements from cryoEM data.

claim: The diameter of the globular portion of UL25 is ~6 nm.
source: The external coats formed in the presence of UL25∆44 Q72A were ~6 nm thicker than the internal NEC coats, and the diameter of the globular portion of UL25 is also ~6 nm.
evidence: This is based on structural information about UL25.

claim: The external coats are composed of a UL25∆44 Q72A layer positioned on top of the membrane-bound NEC220 layer.
source: Therefore, we hypothesize that the external coats are composed of a UL25∆44 Q72A layer positioned on top of the membrane-bound NEC220 layer (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the thickness measurements and structural considerations.

claim: Very few budded vesicles were observed when UL25∆44 Q72A and NEC220 were incubated with LUVs.
source: Very few budded vesicles were observed under these conditions, which is consistent with the inefficient budding observed by confocal microscopy (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations from cryoEM.

claim: Binding of UL25∆44 Q72A to the NEC220 on the surface of the lipid vesicles correlated with its ability to inhibit NEC-mediated budding.
source: Thus, binding of UL25∆44 Q72A to the NEC220 on the surface of the lipid vesicles correlated with its ability to inhibit NEC-mediated budding.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between binding and inhibition observed in the experiments.

claim: Co-incubation of UL25∆73 and NEC220 with LUVs yielded budded vesicles.
source: Co-incubation of UL25∆73 and NEC220 with LUVs yielded budded vesicles (Figure 4b and c)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4b and c.

claim: Some budded vesicles formed by co-incubation of UL25∆73 and NEC220 with LUVs contained ~17 nm thick internal coats.
source: some of which contained ~17 nm thick internal coats (Figure 4c), presumably containing UL25∆73 bound to the NEC220.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4c.

claim: Some budded vesicles formed by co-incubation of UL25∆73 and NEC220 with LUVs contained ~11 nm thick internal coats.
source: We also observed budded vesicles containing ~11 nm thick internal coats (Figure 4b), presumably containing only NEC220, in accordance with our previous report (Bigalke et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4b and a citation to a previous study.

claim: Unbudded LUVs containing >29 nm thick heterogeneous protein aggregates on the external surface were observed when UL25∆73 and NEC220 were co-incubated with LUVs.
source: Last but not least, we observed unbudded LUVs containing >29 nm thick heterogeneous protein aggregates on the external surface (Figure 4d and Figure 4—figure supplement 2)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4d and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: UL25∆44 Q72A formed a net of five-pointed stars covering the surface of membrane-bound NEC220.
source: Sub-tomographic averaging of the 3D reconstructions of unbudded LUVs coated with NEC220 and UL25∆44 Q72A (Figure 5a) revealed that UL25∆44 Q72A formed a net of five-pointed stars (Figure 5c) covering the surface of membrane-bound NEC220
evidence: This is supported by cryoET data shown in Figure 5a and 5c.

claim: Membrane-bound NEC220 formed pentagons when bound to UL25∆44 Q72A.
source: that, in turn, formed pentagons (Figure 5d).
evidence: This is supported by cryoET data shown in Figure 5d.

claim: Five-pointed stars of UL25 were positioned directly on top of the NEC pentagons.
source: Five-pointed stars of UL25 were positioned directly on top of the NEC pentagons (Figure 5c,d).
evidence: This is supported by cryoET data shown in Figure 5c and 5d.

claim: The pentagonal arrangement was observed during averaging even prior to imposing five-fold symmetry.
source: The pentagonal arrangement was observed during averaging even prior to imposing five-fold symmetry (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by cryoET data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Within the NEC220/UL25Δ44 Q72A dataset, only five-fold symmetry was observed in the protruding densities.
source: Within the NEC220/UL25Δ44 Q72A dataset, we only observed five-fold symmetry in the protruding densities, whereas in the NEC220 only dataset, we observed only six-fold symmetry (Figure 5b).
evidence: This is supported by cryoET data shown in Figure 5b.

claim: In the NEC220 only dataset, only six-fold symmetry was observed.
source: Within the NEC220/UL25Δ44 Q72A dataset, we only observed five-fold symmetry in the protruding densities, whereas in the NEC220 only dataset, we observed only six-fold symmetry (Figure 5b).
evidence: This is supported by cryoET data shown in Figure 5b.

claim: When bound to UL25Δ44 Q72A, the NEC220 only forms pentagons and is not a mixture of pentagons and hexagons.
source: Therefore, as far as we can tell, when bound to UL25Δ44 Q72A, the NEC220 only forms pentagons and is not a mixture of pentagons and hexagons.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that only five-fold symmetry is observed in the NEC220/UL25Δ44 Q72A dataset.

claim: The NEC pentagons and hexagons have similar dimensions, ~10.5 nm vs. ~11 nm in width.
source: The NEC pentagons and hexagons have similar dimensions, ~10.5 nm vs. ~11 nm in width (Figure 5b,d) with ~6.5 nm vs. ~6.3 nm sides (Figure 5d; Bigalke et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by measurements from cryoET data shown in Figure 5b and 5d, and a citation to a previous study.

claim: The NEC hexagons are hexamers of the NEC heterodimers.
source: From the crystal structure, we know that the hexagons are hexamers of the NEC heterodimers (Bigalke and Heldwein, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: The NEC pentagons are pentamers of the NEC heterodimers.
source: Therefore, we hypothesize that the pentagons are pentamers of the NEC heterodimers.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the similarity in dimensions between pentagons and hexagons and the knowledge that hexagons are hexamers.

claim: UL25∆44 Q72A/NEC220 spikes did not fully cover the surface of the LUVs, and instead formed patches rather than full coats.
source: Visual analysis of the cryoEM images suggested that UL25∆44 Q72A/NEC220 spikes did not fully cover the surface of the LUVs, and instead formed patches rather than full coats (Figure 4a and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by visual analysis of cryoEM images shown in Figure 4a and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The adjacent NEC pentagons capped with UL25 stars are loosely connected.
source: We hypothesize that the adjacent NEC pentagons capped with UL25 stars are loosely connected, which results in a patchy network of pentagons instead of small, well-defined coats that would form if the arrangement were rigid.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the observation that surrounding pentagons in the sub-tomographic averages are not as sharply defined as the central one.

claim: The cryoET data clearly show the ability of the NEC to form an alternative, pentagonal arrangement in the presence of UL25.
source: Regardless, the cryoET data clearly show the ability of the NEC to form an alternative, pentagonal arrangement in the presence of UL25 thus documenting the ability of the NEC to form different types of oligomers.
evidence: This is supported by the cryoET data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The NEC has the ability to form different types of oligomers.
source: Regardless, the cryoET data clearly show the ability of the NEC to form an alternative, pentagonal arrangement in the presence of UL25 thus documenting the ability of the NEC to form different types of oligomers.
evidence: This is supported by the observation that NEC can form both hexagons and pentagons.

claim: UL25/NEC interactions observed in vitro mimic UL25/NEC interactions that anchor the NEC coat to the capsid vertices.
source: We hypothesize that UL25/NEC interactions observed in vitro mimic UL25/NEC interactions that anchor the NEC coat to the capsid vertices.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the in vitro observations and their potential relevance to the in vivo situation.

claim: NEC pentagons formed at the points of contact with the capsid vertices could nucleate the assembly of the otherwise hexagonal NEC coats and introduce curvature into them.
source: We further hypothesize that NEC pentagons formed at the points of contact with the capsid vertices could nucleate the assembly of the otherwise hexagonal NEC coats and introduce curvature into them.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the observation that NEC can form pentagons when bound to UL25.

claim: The five-pointed UL25 stars formed in vitro resemble the five-pointed stars crowning each capsid vertex that are composed of five copies of the capsid-associated tegument complex (CATC).
source: The five-pointed UL25 stars formed in vitro resemble the five-pointed stars crowning each capsid vertex that are composed of five copies of the capsid-associated tegument complex (CATC) (Dai and Zhou, 2018; Figure 6a).
evidence: This is based on comparison with the cryoEM structure of the HSV-1 capsid, supported by a citation.

claim: Each CATC is composed of two copies of UL25, one copy of UL17, and two copies of the C-terminal portion of the tegument protein UL36.
source: Each CATC, in turn, is composed of two copies of UL25, one copy of UL17, and two copies of the C-terminal portion of the tegument protein UL36 (Dai and Zhou, 2018)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: CATC has a characteristic antiparallel four-helix bundle composed of two UL25 helices and two UL36 helices.
source: and has a characteristic antiparallel four-helix bundle composed of two UL25 helices and two UL36 helices (Figure 6a).
evidence: This is supported by structural information from the cryoEM structure of the HSV-1 capsid.

claim: UL25∆44 Q72A forms an antiparallel four-helix bundle when bound to the NEC220 on the membrane surface in vitro.
source: Therefore, we hypothesize that UL25∆44 Q72A also forms an antiparallel four-helix bundle when bound to the NEC220 on the membrane surface in vitro.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the similarity between the five-pointed stars formed in vitro and those on the capsid.

claim: In the UL25/NEC complex formed in vitro, the helical bundle is composed of two pairs of UL25 helices from adjacent stars.
source: However, in this case, the helical bundle is composed of two pairs of UL25 helices from adjacent stars (Figure 6b), linking them into a net.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the structural modeling shown in Figure 6b.

claim: Each UL25 'star' consists of 10 copies of UL25, with cores arranged in the center and five pairs of helices radiating out.
source: Each UL25 'star' would then consist of 10 copies of UL25, with cores arranged in the center and five pairs of helices radiating out (Figure 6b).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the structural modeling shown in Figure 6b.

claim: UL25∆44 Q72A inhibits NEC220-mediated budding in vitro by binding the membrane-bound NEC and forming five-pointed stars on top of NEC pentagons that are linked into a loose net.
source: We propose that UL25∆44 Q72A inhibits NEC220-mediated budding in vitro by binding the membrane-bound NEC and forming five-pointed stars on top of NEC pentagons that are linked into a loose net (Figure 7b).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the experimental observations and structural modeling.

claim: The UL25/NEC net inhibits budding by restricting conformational changes within the NEC lattice necessary to generate negative membrane curvature.
source: Such a net could inhibit budding by restricting conformational changes within the NEC lattice necessary to generate negative membrane curvature (Figure 7a).
evidence: This is a hypothesis about the mechanism of inhibition.

claim: UL25∆73 does not inhibit budding because it has a much shorter N-terminal helix and cannot form a four-helix bundle.
source: By contrast, UL25∆73 construct does not inhibit budding because it has a much shorter N-terminal helix (Figure 1a) and cannot form a four-helix bundle.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the structural differences between UL25∆44 Q72A and UL25∆73.

claim: UL25∆73 is prone to aggregation likely because the shorter helix is less stable.
source: UL25∆73 is also prone to aggregation likely because the shorter helix is less stable (Figure 7c).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the observed aggregation of UL25∆73.

claim: Free UL25 could inhibit the budding activity of the NEC during infection.
source: It is tempting to speculate that free UL25, which is likely present within the nucleus, could inhibit the budding activity of the NEC during infection.
evidence: This is speculation based on the in vitro observations.

claim: During infection, the NEC budding activity is controlled, presumably by a viral protein, to ensure budding of only mature capsids and to prevent premature, non-productive budding.
source: However, during infection, the NEC budding activity is controlled, presumably by a viral protein, to ensure budding of only mature capsids and to prevent premature, non-productive budding.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation that NEC is constitutively active in vitro but not during infection.

claim: UL31 from HSV-1 infected cell lysates co-immunoprecipitates with UL25.
source: UL31 from HSV-1 infected cell lysates was shown to co-immunoprecipitate with UL25 (Yang and Baines, 2011)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: UL31 binds nucleocapsids.
source: and bind nucleocapsids (Yang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: NEC185∆50 from E. coli binds purified nucleocapsids from HSV-1 infected cells in a pull-down assay.
source: More recently, NEC185∆50 (a previously crystallized truncated construct with an intact membrane-distal UL31 region) from E. coli was shown to bind purified nucleocapsids from HSV-1 infected cells in a pull-down assay (Takeshima et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The interaction between NEC and nucleocapsids requires UL25.
source: This interaction requires UL25 because the VP5, VP23, and UL17 capsid proteins were only detected if UL25 was present on capsids, suggesting NEC binds capsid-bound UL25.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: UL25 likely binds to the membrane-distal tip of UL31.
source: UL25 likely binds to the membrane-distal tip of UL31 because capsid binding to the NEC requires UL31 residues R281 and D282, which are located in this region (Takeshima et al., 2019).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that mutations in this region affect capsid binding, supported by a citation.

claim: Capsid binding to the NEC requires UL31 residues R281 and D282.
source: UL25 likely binds to the membrane-distal tip of UL31 because capsid binding to the NEC requires UL31 residues R281 and D282, which are located in this region (Takeshima et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: In the cryoET reconstruction, UL25 cores sit on the membrane-distal ends of the NEC.
source: In our cryoET reconstruction, UL25 cores sit on the membrane-distal ends of the NEC (Figure 6b).
evidence: This is supported by the cryoET data shown in Figure 6b.

claim: The interactions between UL25 and membrane-bound NEC observed by cryoET in vitro mimic how the NEC interacts with UL25 on the capsid vertices.
source: Therefore, we hypothesize that the interactions between UL25 and membrane-bound NEC that we observed by cryoET in vitro (Figure 6b and d) mimic how the NEC interacts with UL25 on the capsid vertices (Figure 6a and c).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the in vitro observations and their potential relevance to the in vivo situation.

claim: The NEC may be able to tilt relative to the membrane surface.
source: On the other hand, the NEC may be able to tilt relative to the membrane surface (Figure 5a), which would also allow each NEC to adopt the optimal orientation for binding the UL25 cores at the capsid vertices.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the cryoET data shown in Figure 5a.

claim: A strictly hexagonal lattice is flat.
source: A strictly hexagonal lattice is flat, so the curvature is typically achieved through the inclusion of lattice defects, also termed insertions.
evidence: This is established knowledge in structural biology.

claim: No deviations from the hexagonal symmetry have yet been visualized in any NEC coats.
source: Although no deviations from the hexagonal symmetry have yet been visualized in any NEC coats (Bigalke et al., 2014; Hagen et al., 2015; Newcomb et al., 2017)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In perinuclear enveloped virions formed in PRV-infected cells, the NEC coats appear tightly associated with the capsid.
source: In perinuclear enveloped virions formed in PRV-infected cells, the NEC coats appear tightly associated with the capsid (Hagen et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Capsidless perinuclear vesicles formed in uninfected cells expressing PRV NEC are relatively uniform in size (~115 nm in diameter).
source: Capsidless perinuclear vesicles formed in uninfected cells expressing PRV NEC (Hagen et al., 2015) are relatively uniform in size (~115 nm in diameter; Figure 8, inset)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study and shown in Figure 8.

claim: Capsidless perinuclear vesicles are smaller than the capsid (~125 nm in diameter).
source: but smaller than the capsid (~125 nm in diameter Dai and Zhou, 2018; Liu et al., 2017)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Perinuclear enveloped virions isolated from cells infected with the HSV-1 US3-null mutant virus are ~160 nm in diameter.
source: or the perinuclear enveloped virions isolated from cells infected with the HSV-1 US3-null mutant virus (~160 nm in diameter Newcomb et al., 2017; Figure 8).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study and shown in Figure 8.

claim: The capsid appears to define the size of NEC-budded vesicles during infection.
source: The capsid thus appears to define the size of NEC-budded vesicles during infection, so the capsid geometry could influence the geometry of the NEC coat.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that perinuclear enveloped virions are larger than capsidless vesicles.

claim: The capsid geometry could influence the geometry of the NEC coat.
source: The capsid thus appears to define the size of NEC-budded vesicles during infection, so the capsid geometry could influence the geometry of the NEC coat.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that the capsid defines the size of NEC-budded vesicles.

claim: During nuclear egress, NEC pentagons are formed at the points of contact with the capsid vertices.
source: We propose the following model of NEC-mediated capsid budding during nuclear egress in infected cells (Figure 8). Binding of the cores of five neighboring copies of CATC at the capsid vertices to the NEC at the INM would promote formation of NEC pentagons
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the experimental observations.

claim: NEC pentagons serve as a nucleation event for the assembly of the NEC coat around the capsid.
source: which would serve as a nucleation event for the assembly of the NEC coat around the capsid and also help anchor the capsid to the INM.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the experimental observations.

claim: NEC pentagons help anchor the capsid to the INM.
source: which would serve as a nucleation event for the assembly of the NEC coat around the capsid and also help anchor the capsid to the INM.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the experimental observations.

claim: The incorporation of pentagons into the NEC coat at the points of contact with the vertices helps attach the NEC coat to the capsid and introduces curvature into the NEC coat.
source: As the hexagonal NEC coat continues to grow, the incorporation of pentagons into the coat at the points of contact with the vertices would both help attach the NEC coat to the capsid and introduce curvature into the NEC coat (Figure 8).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the experimental observations.

claim: In both HSV-1 and PRV, removal of UL25 results in an accumulation of capsids at the INM, unable to undergo egress.
source: In both HSV-1 and PRV, removal of UL25 results in an accumulation of capsids at the INM, unable to undergo egress (Klupp et al., 2006; Kuhn et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: UL25 both anchors the NEC coat to the capsid and contributes to formation of a curved coat.
source: Our results suggest that UL25 both anchors the NEC coat to the capsid and contributes to formation of a curved coat.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental results presented in the manuscript.

claim: Mostly mature, DNA-containing C-capsids undergo budding at the INM.
source: Additionally, our results could potentially explain why mostly mature, DNA-containing C-capsids undergo budding at the INM (Klupp et al., 2011; Roizman and Furlong, 1974).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: A- and B-capsids have fewer UL25 copies on the capsid surface than C-capsids.
source: A- and B-capsids have fewer UL25 copies on the capsid surface (Newcomb et al., 2006)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Only C-capsids, which contain UL25 at a full occupancy, can generate pentagonal NEC insertions necessary for the formation of an NEC coat around the capsid.
source: and we hypothesize that only C-capsids, which contain UL25 at a full occupancy, can generate pentagonal NEC insertions necessary for the formation of an NEC coat around the capsid.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the experimental observations and the knowledge that C-capsids have more UL25 than A- and B-capsids.

claim: NEC/UL25 interactions could provide a quality-control mechanism that would favor budding of mature, DNA-containing C-capsids over the capsid forms with fewer UL25 copies.
source: In this manner, NEC/UL25 interactions could provide a quality-control mechanism that would favor budding of mature, DNA-containing C-capsids – which have a full UL25 set – over the capsid forms with fewer UL25 copies thereby acting as a checkpoint during nuclear egress.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the experimental observations and the knowledge that C-capsids have more UL25 than A- and B-capsids.

claim: The reported resolution of the cryoET average is 29 Å based on the 0.143 gold-standard FSC criterion.
source: The reported resolution is 29 Å based on the 0.143 gold-standard FSC criterion.
evidence: This is a technical detail about the cryoET data analysis.
